Instant Pot / Pressure Cooker Times

Chicken breasts: 6 to 8 minutes per pound, natural release 10 minutes. Hard-boiled eggs: 5 minutes, 5 minutes natural release, 5 minutes in ice water. Times are at high pressure and don’t include the time to come to pressure.

Times marked without † are from the pressure cooking timetable in the Instant Pot Duo Evo Plus user manual, at high pressure. † marks common recipe times that aren’t in that manual; treat them as starting points. Release types follow the usual practice: quick for vegetables and seafood, natural for meat, beans and grains.

How it works

The times are minutes at pressure. The pot takes another 5 to 15 minutes to build pressure first, depending on how full it is, so plan for that. For meat sold by weight, the calculator multiplies the minutes per pound by your weight. It’s a starting point: check large pieces with a thermometer and give them a few more minutes if they need it. It all runs in your browser. Nothing you type is sent anywhere or saved.

Quick release vs natural release

Quick release means turning the valve to venting as soon as the time is up, which stops the cooking fast. Use it for vegetables and seafood. Natural release means leaving the valve alone while the pressure drops by itself, which keeps cooking the food gently. Meat stays juicier, and beans and grains finish without spitting foam out of the valve.

Ways to use it

  • Weeknight chicken. Breasts from the fridge in about 15 minutes at pressure for 2 lb.
  • Meal-prep beans. Dry black beans in 20 to 25 minutes, no soaking.
  • Rice. 1:1 water, 4 minutes for white.
  • Hard-boiled eggs. The 5-5-5 method peels easily.
  • A frozen roast. Add about half again to the time (see the FAQ).

Questions

What does natural release mean?

You leave the valve closed when the time is up and let the pressure drop by itself. “Natural 10 min” means wait 10 minutes, then turn the valve to release whatever pressure is left. “Natural (full)” means wait until the float valve drops on its own.

Do I count the time to come to pressure?

No. The times are minutes at pressure, after the pot has sealed. Coming up to pressure adds roughly 5 to 15 minutes, more when the pot is full or the food is frozen.

Why are vegetables so short?

Pressure cooking is hot (about 240 °F inside), and vegetables don’t need much to soften. They also keep cooking while the pot comes to pressure, so a 1-minute setting is plenty for broccoli. Use quick release so they don’t turn to mush.

Can I cook frozen meat?

Yes. Cook frozen pieces about 50% longer than the time in the table, and check the center with a thermometer. Frozen pieces stuck together in a block take longer, so separate them if you can.

Is anything saved?

No. The table and calculator run in your browser and nothing is saved or sent anywhere.
